title: GTA VI Reviewers Played 80 Hours to Reach 57%: Rockstar Builds a Game Only Rockstar Can Afford
text:
GTA VI Reviewers Played 80 Hours to Reach 57%: Rockstar Builds a Game Only Rockstar Can Afford — BigGo Finance Ask AI News Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers Earnings Calls Calendar Watchlist Podcasts Influencers More Ask AI News Watchlist Holdings Markets Earnings Calls Calendar Podcasts Influencers GTA VI Reviewers Played 80 Hours to Reach 57%: Rockstar Builds a Game Only Rockstar Can Afford
 Add preferred source The Verge's Andrew Webster spent roughly 80 hours finishing Grand Theft Auto VI's story and found himself only 57% complete — a scale made possible only by a studio whose last two titles sold 230 million and 80 million copies, he argues on The Vergecast. The game wraps a Bonnie-and-Clyde love story around Rockstar's most detailed open world yet, ties free-roaming crime to narrative, and turns the in-game phone into a menu that never pauses. Webster logged just two or three technical faults in 80 hours on a base PlayStation 5, and the relationship and survival mechanics are entirely optional. The financial stakes are enormous: Bank of America says the launch needs at least $1.9 billion in opening sales to satisfy Take-Two investors, and Sensor Tower already pegs preorders near $1 billion. The unresolved question is what becomes of GTA Online, the persistent multiplayer mode that ultimately determines whether GTA VI is a decade-long platform or a finite, very expensive story. Key Elements 
 Rockstar Games Grand Theft Auto VI Take-Two Interactive Software Andrew Webster The Vergecast Grand Theft Auto Online Grand Theft Auto V Red Dead Redemption 2 PlayStation 5 Xbox Series S Strauss Zelnick Bank of America Sensor Tower Digital Foundry Rob Nelson Andrew Webster finished the story in Grand Theft Auto VI, looked at his save file, and discovered he was only 57% done. He had been playing for about 80 hours. That single number tells you most of what you need to know about Rockstar Games' sequel — its size, its ambition, and why no competitor can realistically build anything like it, Webster said on The Vergecast.
 The review copy ran on a base PlayStation 5, played in paced sessions across several weeks rather than marathon stretches, plus one conversation with Rockstar producer Rob Nelson. What emerged from Webster's hands-on account is less a verdict than a map of the design decisions that separate GTA VI from GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2 — and the ones that leave open questions nobody has answered yet.
 The moat is money, and nobody else has it
 Webster's explanation for the 13-year gap between installments isn't perfectionism. It's resource asymmetry. He argues the game is effectively unreplicable because only a studio with Rockstar's back-to-back sales record can fund this level of production.
 "I've said it a bunch — nobody else is trying to make a game like this," he said. "It's, like, literally nobody could make this game. The resources and time necessary is only possible when you have GTA 5 sold, I think, 230 million copies."
 The numbers behind that claim are worth seeing side by side, because they reframe what "a popular game" even means.
 Title Copies sold (Webster's figures) Why it matters here 
 GTA V ~230 million Bankrolls a 13-year development cycle 
 Red Dead Redemption 2 80-plus million Often overlooked, yet among the best-selling games ever 
 Breath of the Wild ~30 million Webster's benchmark for a hit at normal scale 
 Against that backdrop, a 30-million-selling game looks almost modest. Take-Two's own latest quarterly report puts lifetime GTA V sales around 235 million, with the franchise as a whole approaching 480 million units — a foundation that no rival publisher can match, and the reason the sequel's budget buys a world no one else can afford to build.
 Webster reaches for a film analogy: Christopher Nolan directing The Odyssey. The opportunity exists for exactly one filmmaker because nobody else can mount it. The practical consequence is pacing. The first major heist doesn't arrive until roughly 30 hours in — long by reviewer standards, but, as Webster puts it, "a drop in the bucket" for players who spent 13 years inside GTA Online. The game deliberately starts its leads as low-level criminals and scales up to bank robbery, a bet that players will stay for hundreds of hours.
 A love story, with the open world wired into it
 Webster rejects the idea that GTA was ever split between narrative and mayhem — "they're all story games," he says — but argues this entry binds free-roaming activity to the plot more tightly than any predecessor. Jason and Lucia are a couple saving a nest egg to get out. Robbing a store, boosting a car, pulling a heist: each carries a reason rooted in the story. He compares the integration to Red Dead Redemption 2 rather than GTA V's three-protagonist structure.
 "It's literally a love story, it's like Bonnie and Clyde kind of thing," he said. "But then also making that story connect to the things you're doing in the open world in a way that makes sense."
 The old dissonance doesn't vanish. Lucia can gun down 30 cops in a mission and then hold hands with her boyfriend. But the relationship system is optional throughout. Holding hands — an R2 prompt on PlayStation, available once the characters are together, roughly 15 to 16 hours in — improves the relationship and pays off later in the story.
 "You can just walk down the street holding hands and it improves your relationship and if you continue doing it it becomes a meaningful thing in the story later on," Webster said.
 Small gestures carry weight: handing your partner a coffee from a vending machine, or throwing it at them, which damages the relationship. None of it is mandatory. Webster's own experience: "I can't imagine not holding hands with the other person at this point."
 Host David Pierce pushed back that such mechanics turn into a chore by the third repetition. Webster's answer is that the game deliberately refuses to make them a chore.
 "The thing they did that's really smart is just like it's GTA, it should be open and free and that's what it is."
 Hunger and fuel exist but barely bind. A fitness app nags about gains, an apple lasts a couple of days, and Webster never actually ran out of gas. The design serves both audiences — GTA Online veterans who want chaos, and older players who came for the relationship.
 Webster also predicts most players will land somewhere in the middle rather than committing fully to either style: mayhem-first or story-first will be the exception, not the rule.
 The detail is the point — and coffee is the yardstick
 The map sprawls well past Vice City into swamps, the Keys, and a long list of other locations. Webster says it is bigger and more richly detailed than prior Rockstar worlds. He stress-tested non-player characters specifically, since Rockstar reportedly built an entire Los Angeles studio just to produce them. Results varied. Some stranded drivers tell you to get lost. One Amazon-style delivery driver screams that her AI manager will punish her for failed deliveries — a moment that pulled him into a package-delivery storyline.
 The detail runs down to hidden t-shirts in the back rooms of vintage stores. But coffee became his personal instrument for measuring depth, bought from vending machines, restaurants with options, food trucks, or brewed in the apartment — then either shared with a partner or thrown at someone who annoys you.
 "The size of the coffee economy in a game is actually a perfect way to measure the way that that game actually works," Pierce said. "Like the coffee thoughtfulness index feels like a pretty good way to level set whether one of these games is any good."
 Webster expects every player to find their own equivalent obsession. The smartphone is the other structural decision worth studying. It behaves as a menu that doesn't pause anything.
 "It's a menu, but it's part of the world," Webster said. "So like when you pull out your phone, the game doesn't pause. You're walking or driving still."
 The view shifts to first person while you hold it, even mid-drive. Apps interconnect: Lucia texts a meme, tapping it opens an Instagram-like feed with comments you can like and revisit. After a chaotic event, a friend sends a news link, and you can read a five-paragraph article about the chaos you just caused. Webster calls the phone itself forgettable — which he means as a compliment to its realism. Pierce raised the counterpoint that phones ruin most films; Webster's answer is that it's used sparingly, with no doom-scrolling interludes, and mostly as a natural channel for the calls and group chats that used to happen during drives.
 Current, funny, and pointedly not punching down
 Despite the long development, little feels dated. One side quest involves an NFT bro short on cash after the market collapse — "not that far off," Webster says. Artificial intelligence shows up as satire rather than as a system; the AI-manager delivery storyline is his main example, and he suspects a few references were added late to stay current. The radio still carries right-wing talk hosts mocking Brian Johnson, keeping GTA's juvenile streak intact.
 On tone, he says the game skewers plenty but "doesn't really punch down," which he frames as a corrective to a long-standing criticism of the series — with the caveat that he played one very large game and can't speak for all of it.
 Clean on a launch console, with the rough edges left in on purpose
 Webster's technical report is striking for how short it is. On a base PS5, the game looks the way many games' cutscenes look, except you're inside it — convincing enough that a glance could mistake it for stylized real footage. Against the comparison he raises himself, Cyberpunk's disastrous launch, he logged two or three problems in 80 hours: occasional body jittering and one floating coffee cup in the apartment. Repeated NPC chatter and radio lines were rare; it felt, he says, like people talking around him.
 That impression lines up with the broader technical picture. Digital Foundry's early testing found a 30 frames-per-second target holding on the base PS5 through ordinary play, slipping during heavy driving and dropping into the mid-20s in prolonged explosion-heavy firefights. The PS5 Pro holds a steady 30 with consistent frame pacing; the Xbox Series S keeps the 30 FPS target but trades away ray-traced shadows and upscaling, with visibly aliased edges and soft facial detail in one early close-up.
 Mechanical friction is reduced, not eliminated. The weapon wheel "still kind of sucks" — he sometimes pulls a flashlight mid-shootout — and he suspects that's now deliberate. New checkpointing lets players restart later in a failed sequence, and failing enough lets them skip a mission entirely, killing the classic frustration of replaying a 50-enemy shootout or a strict escape route.
 A soundtrack built for people who grew up in the 90s
 Two radio stations are hosted by TLC and by Trina, aimed squarely at listeners born in the 80s and early 90s — "we're the boomers now," Webster says, crediting a colleague named Richard for the line. His favorite music moment is a small one: driving as Jason with Lucia in the passenger seat, switching to a country station, and hearing Lucia complain about how much she hates country music.
 The GTA Online question nobody has answered
 Webster frames the successor to GTA Online as the big unknown, and points to the absence of a Minecraft 2 as evidence that follow-ups to colossal online games are close to impossible. Even pairing GTA VI with the existing GTA Online, he says, probably buys another decade of play. Pierce argues the right call was to push the established formula to untouchable heights rather than branch into something wholly new — and Webster agrees, then notes that Pierce had just handed him the opening for a review he still has to write.
 For Pierce himself, the personal arithmetic is blunt: he says there's a near-100% chance he buys a PlayStation. The game arrived the Thursday after the Monday recording, and the console price at his local Costco climbs about $20 per visit. Webster's reassurance is that a launch-model PS5 ran it fine.
 What the launch is worth
 The commercial machinery around the game is running at a scale to match the world Rockstar built. Sensor Tower estimates preorders at roughly 10.3 million units and about $1 billion in revenue before a single copy sold at retail, with PlayStation taking about 75% of the split. Bank of America has put a number on investor expectations: at least $1.9 billion in opening sales to keep fiscal 2027 guidance intact, with anything below $1.5 billion read as a shortfall against a median expectation of about 50 million units. The stock carries a $330 target from the bank, roughly a third above where it traded in mid-November.
 That framing matters because it shows where the money actually lives. The launch is a spectacle; GTA Online is the annuity. Bank of America models in-game spending near $66 per monthly active user by fiscal 2029, and has pushed its assumption for the next GTA Online to fiscal 2028 — a timing shift, not a doubt. Take-Two chief executive Strauss Zelnick, asked about the year after launch, declined to guide: "I'm not going to give you guidance for fiscal 2028 today."
 Two production facts from Webster's review are worth holding onto. The review process was unusually secretive — which he attributes to Rockstar's history of leaks — though the studio still gave reviewers substantial time with the game. And the generational gap is literal for him: he edited his GTA V review when he had a one-year-old. She is now in high school. The span between the two games is the lifetime of a teenager. He took a break mid-review to play Ocarina of Time, balancing the two at one point.
 The synthesis to carry forward is that GTA VI's achievement isn't a new genre. It's the accumulation of Rockstar's own prior work — GTA V's scale plus Red Dead Redemption 2's density of interaction — executed at a budget no competitor can match. That leaves two variables open. The first is whether the optional relationship and phone systems hold up for players who ignore them; one 80-hour playthrough cannot settle it. The second is what Rockstar does with GTA Online, the piece that decides whether this becomes another decade-long platform or a finite, extraordinarily expensive story. For investors in Take-Two, the launch-weekend sales number is the headline, but the number that shapes the stock through 2027 arrives when players finish the story — and decide whether to keep going.
